name: Poodle hair machine

card.summary: A name for the early-1920s electric permanent-waving machines, with heated rollers hung from an overhead frame, used to give hair lasting waves and curls.
card.note: Early machines risked scalp burns and electrical accidents.

quick.overview:
The 'poodle hair machine' label refers to a 1920 hair-waving apparatus pictured on a woman and her dog, in the era of electric permanent-wave machines. These devices wound hair around heated rollers hung from an overhead stand to set lasting waves.

The appearance goal was curled or wavy hair that lasted for months rather than hours, in contrast to daily tong or rag curling.
quick.how: In the period, a salon operator wound sections of hair around rollers with tubular heaters, applied an alkaline solution and heated the hair, with the apparatus supported on a wheeled stand.
quick.risks: Overheating could damage hair and burn the scalp, and electrical accidents with wet hair were a concern; later designs such as Icall's 1930s wireless system kept electricity away from the head [1].

lead: Early electric permanent-wave machines of the 1910s and 1920s are the context for the 'poodle hair machine' image. Karl Nessler demonstrated his method on 8 October 1905 using rods connected to an electric heater and a caustic solution, with counterweights hung from overhead to keep heavy rollers off the scalp; early trials burned his wife's hair and scalp [1].

From 1917, Isidoro Calvete's heater design, patented by Eugene Suter, heated hair near the root more than the ends; 1920s machines used tubular heaters over rollers on a wheeled stand with a circular 'chandelier', processing up to about 22 sections at once [1].

chain: Hair wound on heated rollers with alkaline solution
angle.text: The process set waves into hair that persisted for weeks to months, a lasting change in hairstyle compared with temporary curling.

infobox: Karl Nessler (1905), Eugene Suter and Isidoro Calvete (1917) [1]

paras: Marcel Grateau created the first practical thermal waving method in 1872 using heated tongs [1]. Nessler's 1905 machine was used in London by 1909 [1]. Suter and Calvete's competing companies, Eugene Ltd and Icall, produced rival machines [1]. Point winding, reportedly introduced by Josef Mayer around 1924, used croquignole heaters clipped onto the hair [1].
